answer: HYPOTHESIS — answered: In the replication-heterogeneity dataset, Economics is the only domain where the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies. At the study level (one ratio per O/R pair, after excluding the 118 `drop==True` rows and using the project-published `aggregated==True` row for the 26 multi-lab Many Labs ids), Economics has mean authors_male.o = 0.87 (author-weighted 0.88; 77.8% of studies with ratio > 0.5) and mean authors_male.r = 0.84 (author-weighted 0.81; 72.2% of studies > 0.5) — both clearly and substantially above 0.5 on every aggregation. Social and Cognitive exceed 0.5 on the original-paper side but fail on the replication side (study-level Social R mean 0.50 / fraction > 0.5 = 48.4%; Cognitive R mean 0.52 / fraction > 0.5 = 44.9%). Economics has n=18 O/R pairs (small sample), but its replication-side margin above 0.5 is ~0.34, large enough that the conclusion is unlikely to flip with a few more studies. The conclusion is robust to the per-row sensitivity check (averaging across all 927 per-lab rows) and to author-weighting.

payload.hypothesis: In the replication-heterogeneity dataset, the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies in the Economics domain. After excluding the 118 `drop==True` rows (all Social) and re-expressing the data with one ratio per unique O/R pair (using the project-published `aggregated==True` row for the 26 Many Labs multi-lab ids), Economics has mean authors_male.o = 0.87 (author-weighted 0.88; 77.8% of studies with ratio > 0.5) and mean authors_male.r = 0.84 (author-weighted 0.81; 72.2% of studies with ratio > 0.5) — above 0.5 on both sides for every aggregation we report. Social and Cognitive are majority-male on the original-paper side (means 0.66 and 0.71; weighted 0.64–0.71) but their replication-side central tendencies hover at or below 0.5 (study-level Social R mean 0.50, fraction > 0.5 = 48.4%; Cognitive R mean 0.52, fraction > 0.5 = 44.9%), so they do not satisfy the joint criterion. Economics has only n=18 O/R pairs (small sample), but the replication-side margin (~0.34 above 0.5) is large enough that the conclusion is unlikely to flip. The per-row sensitivity check (no id-collapse, 809 rows after drop filter) gives a consistent picture (Economics R mean 0.84, both Cognitive and Social R means < 0.55). File 2 (/meta-regression_replication_success_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv) does not contain discipline or authors_male columns and is not used in this analysis.
payload.workflow: 1) Load data/meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv (927x57) and verify schema — all 57 columns present and clean. 2) Drop the 118 rows where drop==True (all Social). 3) Collapse to one ratio per unique `id` (141 -> 131 ids after the drop filter). For the 26 Many Labs / multi-row ids, use the single aggregated==True row whose authors_male.r is the project-published study-level value. 4) For each discipline compute three central tendencies of authors_male.o and authors_male.r: unweighted mean across ids; author-weighted mean = sum(ratio * n_authors) / sum(n_authors); fraction of ids with ratio > 0.5. 5) Mark a discipline as 'majority-male' on side s iff all three aggregations exceed 0.5; the answer must clear both sides. 6) Sensitivity: repeat on the per-row data (no id-collapse). 7) Verify with the script artifacts/analysis.py — output also stored as artifacts/result.json.
